headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Under-Water Seal Drainage
headings.content: Under-water seal drainage is a critical intervention utilized in thoracic nursing to restore and maintain normal negative intrapleural pressure, allowing the lungs to expand fully following surgery, trauma, or medical illness. The intrapleural space normally maintains a negative pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, preventing lung collapse. When air, blood, fluid, or purulent exudate accumulates in this space due to conditions like pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pleural effusion, the lung is compressed and respiratory compromise ensues. The primary principle of the under-water seal system relies on a one-way valve mechanism, typically created by submerging the distal end of a chest catheter two centimeters below sterile water in a collection chamber. This water seal permits the escape of air and drainage from the patient's pleural cavity during expiration and coughing, while preventing the backflow of atmospheric air and fluid into the thorax during inspiration. Gravity drainage assists fluid removal, and optional suction can be applied to accelerate evacuation. For nursing students in Nigeria practicing in diverse clinical settings, understanding this fluid dynamics principle is essential for maintaining patient safety, preventing tension pneumothorax, and ensuring effective respiratory recovery. Constant vigilance over the bubbling and fluctuation patterns within the water seal chamber provides immediate insight into the patient's intrapleural dynamics and system integrity.

headings.title: Indications for Chest Tube Insertion
headings.content: Chest tube insertion is indicated whenever the normal negative pressure of the pleural space is disrupted by the abnormal accumulation of air, blood, chyle, or serous fluid. Recognizing these clinical indications is a core competency for nursing students caring for cardiothoracic and trauma patients. The most common indication is a pneumothorax, which can be spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic, where air enters the pleural space and causes partial or complete lung collapse. A tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening medical emergency requiring immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion to relieve escalating intrathoracic pressure that compromises venous return and cardiac output. Another major indication is a hemothorax or hemopneumothorax, typically resulting from chest trauma, cardiothoracic surgery, or malignancy, where blood fills the pleural cavity. Pleural effusions and empyema also necessitate chest drainage to remove symptomatic serous fluid or infected purulent material, respectively, thereby improving pulmonary ventilation and resolving infection. Prophylactic chest tube placement is routinely performed following open-heart surgeries, lobectomies, and other major thoracic procedures to continuously drain post-operative blood and air. Prompt identification of signs and symptoms such as dyspnea, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, and asymmetrical chest expansion allows nurses to anticipate and prepare for emergency chest tube insertion.

headings.title: Types of Chest Drainage Systems
headings.content: Modern chest drainage systems have evolved from traditional three-bottle setups into integrated, disposable plastic units that combine multiple functions into a single compact device. Understanding the structure of these systems is crucial for safe nursing practice. The classic system consists of three distinct chambers: the collection chamber, the water seal chamber, and the suction control chamber. The collection chamber receives and measures fluid draining from the patient's pleural cavity, featuring calibrated columns that allow nurses to accurately document hourly or daily drainage volumes and characteristics. The water seal chamber contains the water column that acts as a one-way valve, preventing air from re-entering the chest while allowing monitoring of tidaling (the rise and fall of water with respiration) and air leaks (bubbling). The third chamber is the suction control chamber, which can be wet or dry. In wet suction systems, the water level in this chamber determines the amount of negative pressure transmitted to the patient, regardless of wall suction intensity. Dry suction systems use a built-in mechanical regulator or dial to control suction levels without water, offering greater consistency and eliminating evaporation concerns. Familiarity with both traditional glass systems and modern dry-suction disposable units ensures that nurses can safely manage whichever equipment is available in their healthcare facility.

headings.title: Pre-Procedural and Procedural Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content: Preparing a patient for chest tube insertion and managing the immediate procedural phase requires meticulous nursing care, patient education, and adherence to infection control protocols. Before the procedure, the nurse must ensure that informed consent has been obtained from the patient or legally authorized representative. The nurse explains the procedure in simple, reassuring terms to alleviate anxiety, noting that local anesthesia will be used to minimize pain, though pressure and pushing sensations may be felt. Essential equipment must be gathered at the bedside, including the chest drainage system, sterile water, connecting tubing, a thoracostomy tray, local anesthetic, suture materials, occlusive dressings (such as petroleum gauze), and emergency airway supplies. Vital signs and baseline respiratory assessment must be documented prior to insertion. During the procedure, the nurse assists the physician or surgeon by maintaining sterile technique, monitoring the patient's physiological status, offering emotional support, and observing for signs of distress, hypoxia, or vasovagal response. Immediately after insertion, the nurse connects the chest tube to the drainage system, secures all connections with waterproof tape or cable ties to prevent accidental disconnection, tapes the tube to the chest wall to reduce tension, and applies a sterile occlusive dressing around the insertion site. Obtaining a stat post-procedure chest X-ray is vital to confirm proper lung expansion and correct tube placement.

headings.title: Ongoing Assessment and Monitoring of the Patient
headings.content: Ongoing assessment and monitoring form the bedrock of safe nursing care for patients with chest drainage systems. The nurse must perform systematic respiratory assessments at least every two to four hours, evaluating breath sounds, respiratory rate and depth, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, and chest wall symmetry. Diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side may indicate unresolved pneumothorax, lung collapse, or tube occlusion. The nurse evaluates the insertion site and surrounding chest wall for subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus), which feels like rice crispies under the skin and indicates air leaking into the subcutaneous tissue. The dressing must be inspected regularly to ensure it remains clean, dry, and securely occlusive. Pain management is crucial because pleuritic chest pain can inhibit deep breathing and coughing, leading to atelectasis; nurses should administer prescribed analgesics proactively before repositioning or physiotherapy. The drainage system itself must be checked continuously: ensure it remains upright, below the level of the patient's chest at all times to prevent backflow of fluid into the pleural space, and that tubing is free of kinks, loops, or dependent loops that could obstruct drainage. Documenting the color, consistency, and exact volume of output at the end of every shift is mandatory, reporting any sudden surges of bright red blood or unexpected cessation of drainage immediately.

headings.title: Management and Maintenance of the Drainage System
headings.content: Proper management and maintenance of the under-water seal drainage system prevent complications and ensure continuous therapeutic efficacy. Nurses must understand how to interpret the behaviors of fluid within the system's chambers. Tidaling, the vertical movement of water in the water seal chamber corresponding with the patient's respiratory cycle (rising with inspiration, falling with expiration), is normal and indicates that the system is patent and communicating freely with the pleural space. If tidaling stops unexpectedly, it may mean the lung has fully re-expanded, or it could indicate an obstruction, kinking, or dependent loop in the tubing. Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber indicates an air leak within the system or patient circuit, whereas intermittent bubbling is normal during exhalation, coughing, or sneezing in patients with a pneumothorax. To locate an air leak, the nurse can briefly clamp the tubing close to the chest wall; if bubbling stops, the leak is inside the patient's chest or at the insertion site. If bubbling continues, the nurse systematically checks connections down the tubing toward the unit. Milking or stripping chest tubes is generally discouraged today due to the dangerously high negative pressures it creates, which can damage lung tissue and provoke bleeding; instead, gentle hand-over-hand coiling and expressing of clots is used only when specifically ordered and clinically indicated. Maintaining strict infection control during dressing changes and unit replacements is vital to prevent empyema.

headings.title: Troubleshooting and Emergency Interventions
headings.content: Emergency preparedness is a critical nursing skill when managing patients with chest drainage systems, as sudden complications can be life-threatening. The nurse must keep specific emergency equipment at the bedside at all times: two rubber-tipped (hemostat) clamps, a bottle of sterile normal saline or sterile water, and extra sterile dressings. If the chest tube accidentally disconnects from the drainage system, the nurse should immediately submerge the open end of the tubing approximately two centimeters into the bottle of sterile water to re-establish a temporary water seal, preventing atmospheric air from entering the pleural space, and then obtain a new drainage unit. If the chest tube is accidentally pulled completely out of the patient's chest, the nurse must immediately apply a sterile petroleum gauze or occlusive dressing taped on three sides, which allows trapped air to escape during exhalation while preventing air entry during inspiration, and notify the attending physician urgently. In the rare event that the drainage unit cracks or breaks, the nurse quickly places the distal end of the connecting tubing into sterile water. If tension pneumothorax develops due to an obstruction or clamped tube, manifested by sudden respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, and hemodynamic instability, the nurse must unclamp the tubing immediately and notify the physician. Maintaining composure, following established unit protocols, and taking swift corrective action save lives during thoracic emergencies.

headings.title: Chest Tube Removal and Post-Removal Care
headings.content: Chest tube removal is performed when the underlying pathology has resolved, evidenced by complete lung re-expansion on chest X-ray, cessation of air leak (no bubbling in the water seal chamber), and minimal fluid drainage (typically less than 100 to 200 mL per 24 hours, depending on protocol). The nurse plays a vital role in preparing the patient, assisting the provider during removal, and providing meticulous post-removal care. Prior to removal, the nurse explains the procedure, administers prescribed analgesics 30 to 60 minutes beforehand to minimize discomfort, and gathers supplies including suture removal kits, sterile gauze, petroleum dressings, wide adhesive tape, and a biohazard waste bag. During the procedure, the patient is instructed to take a deep breath, hold it, and bear down (Valsalva maneuver), or take a deep breath and exhale fully depending on institutional guidelines; this maneuver increases intrathoracic pressure and prevents air from being sucked back into the pleural space as the tube is rapidly withdrawn. The clinician immediately applies an airtight petroleum gauze and occlusive dressing over the insertion site, secured tightly with tape. Post-removal nursing responsibilities include monitoring vital signs and respiratory status every 15 minutes for the first hour, then hourly, assessing for signs of recurrent pneumothorax or hemothorax (such as dyspnea, decreased breath sounds, or chest pain), inspecting the dressing for excessive drainage or bleeding, and comforting the patient. A follow-up chest X-ray is typically ordered within hours of removal to confirm sustained lung expansion.
